div.p: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable evaluation in Japanese, we carefully localize tau-bench through machine translation, entity adaptation, and human review. During this process, we also uncover and fix two flaws in the original tau-bench: invalid tasks and a score aggregation error that inflates certain models' results. Experiments show that J-tau yields fewer evaluation errors than a naively machinetranslated counterpart and that our fixes resolve both flaws.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Large language model (LLM) agents that autonomously use tools to solve complex tasks have attracted growing attention (Wang et al., 2024). While many benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate such agents, most of them focus on English. Because agent performance can vary across languages (Hofman et al., 2026), English evaluations may not reflect utility in other languages.

To address this gap, multilingual agent benchmarks have been proposed, including ones built from multilingual corpora and machine translations of English benchmarks (Kulkarni et al., 2025;Nguyen et al., 2026). However, machine translation alone cannot localize entities such as personal names, which can lead to unnatural conversations or even invalid tasks (Kim et al., 2026).

To overcome these limitations, we present and release J-tau, a Japanese extension of the widely used English benchmark τ -bench (tau-bench) (Yao et al., 2025;Barres et al., 2026;Cuadron et al., 2025). J-tau is the first publicly available Japanese benchmark that evaluates tool-using LLM agents in realistic, interactive scenarios. It features highquality localization (Fig. 1) and corrected tasks and evaluation. Our main contributions are as follows:

• We construct and release J-tau, a Japanese benchmark that localizes three domains of tau-bench. • We identify two flaws in tau-bench and fix them in J-tau: invalid tasks (about 10% in airline and retail) and score-inflating aggregation (up to 64.6 points for a single model). • We show that an existing machine-translationbased pipeline often causes evaluation failures that stem from the framework rather than agents.

div.head: Background: tau-bench
div.p: This section describes tau-bench and its limitations, along with prior work addressing them. 1

div.head: Overview
div.p: tau-bench is a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on customer support tasks across multiple domains, including airline (booking flights), retail (modifying orders), and telecom (troubleshooting mobile phones). In each task, an LLM-simulated user follows a user instruction describing its goal, and the agent must resolve the request conversationally, calling tools while complying with a domain-specific policy. In telecom, as in realworld technical support, the user has a separate set of tools, so the agent must also guide the user in using them.

div.head: Limitations
div.p: tau-bench has three main limitations. First, it is English-centric. While prior work extends it to five other languages 2 (Nguyen et al., 2026), this extension relies primarily on machine translation, which degrades data quality and leads to unnatural conversations. 3 Second, although tau-bench has been revised since its release (Cuadron et al., 2025), it still contains invalid tasks that are unsolvable or have non-deterministic ground truths. Third, its score aggregation is flawed and overestimates the performance of some models.

div.head: Japanese Agent Benchmark: J-tau
div.p: This section describes the construction pipeline and details of J-tau, a Japanese agent benchmark 1 See Appendix A for additional related work. 2 Mandarin, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, and Filipino. 3 For example, users converse in a Southeast Asian language, yet addresses and currencies remain those of the U.S. that addresses the limitations of tau-bench.foot_0

div.head: Construction Pipeline
div.p: Our pipeline consists of five steps (see Fig. 2): three for Japanese localization (translation, entity adaptation, and human review) and two for fixing evaluation issues (task fixes and scoring fixes).

Step 1: LLM Translation. We translate the policies, tool definitions, databases, and user instructions from English into Japanese using Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google DeepMind, 2026). To ensure consistent translation of technical terms, we include a predefined domain-specific glossary in the prompt. Appendix B.1 shows the domain-specific glossaries.

Step 2: Entity Adaptation. Direct translation retains locale-specific entities from Englishspeaking regions, such as personal names, addresses, and phone numbers, making the simulated conversations unnatural for Japanese speakers. We therefore replace them with fictitious Japanese counterparts. We generate them with Fakerfoot_1 for the retail and airline domains, which contain many users, and create them manually for the telecom domain. We also convert monetary amounts into Japanese yen (1 USD = 150 JPY) and the time zone from EST to JST (see Appendix B.2 for more details).

Step 3: Human Review. We then assess and correct the translation quality of the resulting data. For each domain, three experts review the policies, and for the airline and retail domains, experts also review the user instructions (see Appendix B.3).

Step 4: Fix Tasks. We verify each task through manual inspection and test runs, and identify tasks that cannot be solved. 6 We find two types of problematic tasks: tasks that become unsolvable through localization, and invalid tasks already present in the original tau-bench, which are unsolvable or have non-deterministic ground truths. 7 We fix these tasks in J-tau, for example by adding missing information to the user instructions (see Appendix B.4).

Step 5: Fix Scoring. tau-bench treats both empty responses and tool calls with malformed JSON as infrastructure errors. It retries them up to three times and excludes trials with persistent errors from aggregation. However, agent errors reflect the agent's limitations, so this procedure inflates the scores of models prone to such errors. 8 In J-tau, we instead attribute these errors to the model that produced them. Trials are counted as failures for agent errors and discarded for user simulator errors.

div.head: Benchmark Details
div.p: Constructed through this pipeline, J-tau is a highquality Japanese agent benchmark covering the airline, retail, and telecom domains. 9 In interactive agent evaluation, the choice of user simulator can substantially affect agent scores (Seshadri et al., 2026). We therefore compare several recent LLMs in terms of Japanese naturalness and instruction-following stability, and adopt GLM-5.2-FP8 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), which distorted evaluation results the least, as the default user simulator (see Appendix I).

div.p: In this section, we evaluate and analyze a range of proprietary and open-weight models on J-tau.

div.head: Effect of Task and Scoring Fixes
div.p: We conduct an ablation study to assess the effectiveness of the task and scoring fixes in our pipeline in Section 3.1. To this end, we use tau-bench * (tau * ), a variant of tau-bench (tau) to which only the scoring fix in Step 5 is applied.

Fix Tasks. To examine the effect of the task fixes in Step 4, we split tasks into Repaired and Unmodified groups. Table 3: Effect of the scoring fix, comparing tau and tau * for each domain (mean over three trials).

On the Repaired tasks, high-performing models score substantially higher on J-tau than on tau * . This is because the invalid tasks in tau * cap the achievable accuracy regardless of model capability, and our fixes remove this cap. On the Unmodified tasks, which allow a direct comparison between languages, J-tau scores tend to be lower than tau * scores. This is consistent with Hofman et al.
(2026), who show that agent performance varies across languages.

Fix Scoring. To examine the effect of the scoring fix in Step 5, Table 3 compares scores on tau and tau * . For high-performing models, the difference is small. However, for small models such as Qwen3.5-4B, scores drop substantially on tau * , which counts empty and malformed outputs as failures. Thus, tau-bench inflates the scores of such models.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We presented J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for interactive tool-using LLM agents. Beyond machine translation, we localized tau-bench through entity adaptation and human review, and fixed its invalid tasks and a scoring flaw, enabling more accurate evaluation. Our analysis showed that machine translation alone increases framework-caused failures. We hope Jtau advances Japanese LLM agents and our insights benefit benchmark localization for other languages.

div.head: Limitations
div.p: • J-tau covers three domains (airline, retail, and telecom) and does not include the bank-ing_knowledge domain introduced in the latest version of tau-bench (Shi et al., 2026). • J-tau covers only Japanese and cannot be used to evaluate agents in other languages. Concurrent work released within one month before our submission extends tau-bench to more languages (Kuang et al., 2026;Ray et al., 2026b), but these benchmarks may still contain the invalid tasks and the aggregation flaw we identify (Appendix A). Since our task and scoring fixes are language-independent, extending our pipeline to other languages is left for future work. • Addresses and other user information in the airline and retail domains are generated with Faker and thus include nonexistent place names and addresses, limiting their fidelity to real-world data. • Because the solvability verification in Step 4 (Section 3.1) relies only on GLM-5.2-FP8, it may reflect biases specific to this model, and a small number of invalid tasks may remain undetected. • As shown in Section 5.2, J-tau has more failures attributed to the user simulator than SEATau ja , especially in the retail domain. This is likely because the user simulator follows the user simulation guideline less faithfully in Japanese than in English (see Appendix G.5 for an ablation study). Since this may change as models improve, revisiting the choice of user simulator is left for future work. • The original tau-bench prompt instructs models to produce outputs in JSON format. During evaluation after constructing J-tau, we found that this instruction affects some models, such as Kimi-K3 (Kimi Team et al., 2026), more strongly in Japanese, causing them to output JSON strings instead of natural-language responses to the user. Since these outputs are counted as failures, the scores of such models may be underestimated (see Appendix H.2 for an ablation study). We plan to remove this instruction in the revised version.

div.head: Ethical Considerations
div.p: J-tau contains no personally identifiable information, as all user information, such as names, addresses, and phone numbers, is fictitious. The human review was conducted by in-house annotators as part of their regular duties, for which they received their standard salaries.

div.head: A Additional Related Work
div.p: Agent benchmarks. LLM agent evaluation has evolved from static tasks that check single-turn function calls and their arguments (Patil et al., 2025) to challenging multi-step tasks requiring advanced reasoning and environment interaction (Jimenez et al., 2024;Sun et al., 2026). Among such benchmarks, tau-bench (Yao et al., 2025;Barres et al., 2026;Shi et al., 2026) evaluates agents on customer-support tasks in which they resolve the requests of an LLM-simulated user through multi-turn conversations, calling tools while complying with domain policies.

Multilingual agent benchmarks. Some studies build tasks grounded in each language and culture (Almeida et al., 2025;Li et al., 2026;Zhou et al., 2025;Lee et al., 2026), while others translate existing English benchmarks (Hofman et al., 2026;Caciolai et al., 2026;Luo et al., 2026). The validity of the latter has been questioned: Hofman et al. ( 2026) report degraded agent performance in non-English languages on their machine-translated benchmarks, whereas Kim et al. (2026) show that much of this gap stems from translation artifacts rather than model capability.

div.head: B.2 Entity Adaptation
div.p: In the entity adaptation of Step 2, we create a mapping from the original entities in the user information, such as personal names, addresses, phone numbers, and user IDs, to fictitious entities suited to Japanese culture. For the retail domain, we build a dictionary of product names and product variants and replace them accordingly to ensure consistent translations. For the airline domain, we replace the airports with domestic Japanese airports to keep the geographic setting consistent with the conversation language. Table 7 shows the airport mapping. We convert monetary amounts into Japanese yen at 1 USD = 150 JPY and round them to the nearest yen, since fractional yen are not used in everyday transactions. We also change the time zone from EST to JST. Because the agent passes Japanese values to the tools in J-tau, we apply this localization not only to the surface text but also to DB values, enumerated values of tool arguments, and values accepted by the tool implementations, consistently converting them into Japanese according to the glossaries and mappings.

div.head: B.4 Fix Tasks
div.p: Task fixing consists of two stages: addressing issues caused by localization and repairing invalid tasks in the original tau-bench. First, we identify tasks that become unsolvable or whose characteristics, such as difficulty, change substantially through localization. To this end, we manually inspect the task instructions and evaluation criteria of all tasks. Table 9 lists the modified tasks.
Next, to find invalid tasks in the original tau-bench, we run each task three times with GLM-5.2-FP8 and examine its behavior, focusing on tasks that fail two or more times.

div.head: G Details of the Experiments with SEATau
div.p: This section provides details of the comparison between J-tau and SEATau ja in Section 5.2. First, we describe the construction of SEATau ja with the SEATau pipeline and its evaluation results. Next, we describe the setup of the failure cause analysis.
We then examine why SEATau ja achieves higher scores than J-tau in the telecom domain, and why it has fewer user simulator failures. Finally, we present example simulations.

div.head: G.1 Construction of SEATau ja
div.p: We construct SEATau ja with the SEATau pipeline (Nguyen et al., 2026)foot_3 using Gemini 3.1 Pro. As with tau * , we apply only the scoring fix in Step 5 to the SEATau evaluation framework so that the results of SEATau ja are comparable with those of J-tau. SEATau allows control over which components are in the target language, and we adopt the l2_domain scenario, which has the widest translation scope. In this scenario, the simulation is run with the conversations, tool documentation, policies, database, and task definitions all in the target language.

div.head: G.2 Evaluation on SEATau ja
div.p: We use the same evaluation settings as J-tau, with GLM-5.2-FP8 as the user simulator and gpt-oss-120b as the LLM judge for the retail domain.

Table 25 compares the results on J-tau and SEATau ja . In the airline and retail domains, most models score lower on SEATau ja than on J-tau, and Kimi-K3 is the only model that scores higher in both domains. As shown in Table 4, this is likely because SEATau ja has many framework-caused failures in these domains.

In contrast, in the telecom domain, many models score higher on SEATau ja than on J-tau. Since telecom tasks are programmatically generated, framework issues like those in the airline and retail domains are unlikely to occur. Instead, the higher scores are likely due to the additional instructions in the SEATau system prompts, which we discuss in Appendix G.4.

Note that Kimi-K3 consistently scores higher on SEATau ja than on J-tau. This is likely due to the Japanese translation of the JSON-output instruction inherited from tau-bench, which we discuss in Appendix H.2.

div.head: G.3 Setup of the Failure Cause Analysis
div.p: For the failure cause analysis in Section 5.2, we use Sol as an LLM judge. For each failed trial, we provide the scenario, evaluation criteria, and conversation transcript, and have the model classify the cause as the agent, user simulator, or evaluation framework. Figures 3 and4 show the system and user prompts, respectively.

div.head: G.4 Cause of Higher Telecom Scores on SEATau ja
div.p: The SEATau evaluation environment adds its own instructions to the system prompts of both the agent and the user simulator. Figure 5 shows the system prompts used in SEATau ja , with the added instructions in red. Among them are instructions on handling user-side tools: the agent should ask the user to perform such actions rather than call them itself, and the user simulator should call its tools rather than describe the actions in prose.
Since the telecom domain is the only domain with user-side tools, these instructions likely explain the higher telecom scores in Table 25.

div.head: G.5 Cause of Fewer User Simulator Failures on SEATau ja
div.p: As shown in Table 4, SEATau ja has fewer failures attributed to the user simulator than J-tau, especially in the retail domain. The two benchmarks differ in the system prompt of the user simulator: J-tau provides the user simulation guideline

div.head: System Prompt
div.p: You are an adjudicator for agent-benchmark evaluations. You are given a simulation record from a Japanese-language tau2-bench. The record contains the task's user-scenario instructions, the evaluation criteria, the policy given to the agent, and the conversation transcript (user utterances / agent utterances with tool calls / tool responses).
This simulation was scored 0. Read the record and determine: whether this failure is due to the agent itself, the user model, or the evaluation harness.
Failure-cause vocabulary (primary_cause: exactly one; secondary_causes: zero or more):

-agent_error : a genuine error by the model itself (wrong operation, policy violation, providing wrong information, missing actions, transferring to a human too early, etc.). The same failure would occur even with a correctly working harness.

-value_space_mismatch : the values accepted by the tool/runtime (enums, fixed strings) are inconsistent with the language or values of the scenario instructions, so an operation that looks correct fails with a tool error -language_mismatch : the agent switched to English, or the system instructions were in English, etc.; a language inconsistency caused the dialogue or the NL-assertion scoring to fail -user_sim_issue : suspicious behavior of the user simulator itself (misinformation, contradictions, uncooperative loops, clearly untranslated responses) is the direct cause of the failure -env_db_issue : caused by an inconsistency in the DB or environment data -eval_criteria_issue : a defect in the evaluation criteria itself (an unsolvable task, missing or inconsistent criteria, a suspected scoring-logic bug) -other : none of the above Verdict:

-verdict: "valid_failure" (the failure judgment is legitimate), "user_induced" (the user caused the failure; the agent's handling is not necessarily bad), "harness_induced" (a harness-side defect caused the failure; the agent's handling is not necessarily bad), "uncertain" Notes:
-Treat the scoring rationale provided by the harness (justification, etc.) as reference only and verify it independently. Do not take it at face value.
-If a tool response contains an error (e.g., {"error": true, "error_code": "tool_error", ...}), identify the cause by comparing the error content with the arguments the model passed.
-An agent's utterances switching to English can itself serve as evidence for language_mismatch, but judge separately whether it was the direct cause of the failure.

To examine the effect of this difference, we construct J-tau en-user , a variant of J-tau that keeps its task scenarios but otherwise uses the same user simulator system prompt as SEATau ja .

Table 26 shows the results in the retail domain. For all models, J-tau en-user reduces user simulator failures by about half or more relative to J-tau, yielding even fewer than SEATau ja . These results suggest that SEATau ja has fewer user simulator failures because the user simulator follows the guideline more faithfully in English than in Japanese. Indeed, most user simulator failures on J-tau stem from ending the conversation before the task is completed, and when to end the conversation is specified only in the guideline.

Nevertheless, we keep the guideline in Japanese to maintain the full localization of J-tau. Since user simulators are expected to follow Japanese instructions better as models improve, revisiting the choice of user simulator is left for future work, as noted in the Limitations section.

div.head: H Additional Analyses
div.p: This section presents two additional analyses of how the evaluation settings of J-tau affect agent scores. Appendix H.1 examines the effect of the tool language by evaluating a configuration that keeps the tool-related components in English, as is common in real-world applications. Appendix H.2 examines the effect of the system prompt inherited from tau-bench, focusing on Kimi-K3, whose score drops substantially only on J-tau.

div.head: H.1 Effect of Tool Language
div.p: In real-world applications, tools are often defined in English even when the agent converses in Japanese with users in Japan. To reproduce this setting, we construct J-tau en-tool (Table 11) for the telecom domain, which keeps the tool descriptions, argument values, return values, and error messages in English. Tool-related terms in the policies and task scenarios are also kept in English, while the conversation and locale-specific entities remain the same as in J-tau.
Table 29 shows the results. For models with sufficient capability, keeping the tool definitions in English does not substantially degrade agent performance.

div.head: H.2 Effect of System Prompt
div.p: Kimi-K3 scores substantially lower on J-tau than on tau * and SEATau ja (Tables 3 and25). Analyzing its conversations, we find that this drop is due to Kimi-K3 often responding to the user in JSON format, which occurs only on J-tau. We suspect that this behavior is caused by the instruction in the tau-bench system prompt to output in JSON format. As shown in Table 30, removing this instruction improves the score of Kimi-K3 in the telecom domain from 67.0 to 84.8, closing most of the gap with tau * (88.9). Since tau * and SEATau ja also contain this instruction but in English, this suggests that the instruction affects Kimi-K3 more strongly when written in Japanese, causing it to ignore the required output format. Although this instruction is inherited from tau-bench, it is inconsistent with the evaluation framework, and we plan to remove it in the revised version, as noted in the Limitations section. To assess the quality of the user simulator, we evaluate user behavior in simulated conversations using the conversation review feature of tau-bench. We use Sol as an LLM judge to classify the errors in each user utterance by type and severity, based on the user instructions and the conversation. Besides the existing error types, such as hal-lucination, instruction violation, missing required actions, and premature disclosure of information, we introduce a new type for non-fluent Japanese output. As evaluation metrics, we use the percentage of simulations with any user error (err%) and the percentage of simulations with critical errors that affect the evaluation result (crit%).

div.head: I Selection of the User Simulator
div.p: As candidate user simulators, we select openweight models that can run on eight H100 GPUs. Specifically, we use Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 (Qwen Team, 2025) 13 , which is used in existing leaderboards such as Artificial Analysis 14 , as well as GLM-5.2-FP8 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 (Appendix E), which achieve high scores on tau-bench. As agents, we use these two highperforming models as well as Qwen3.5-9B, a smaller and weaker model, to verify that the user simulator also behaves appropriately with less capable agents. Table 31 shows the results with these three agents.

GLM-5.2-FP8 consistently achieves the lowest error rates with all three agents. Its error rates are not lower with the GLM-5.2-FP8 agent than with the other agents, showing no bias in favor of an agent of the same model. Therefore, we adopt GLM-5.2-FP8 as the user simulator for J-tau.
